title: Supreme Court Stays CMRL Probe Against Pinarayi Vijayan for One Week
excerpt: A vacation bench paused the investigation — not the FIR — so the former Kerala chief minister, his daughter Veena T and son-in-law P A Mohamed Riyas can appeal to the High Court division bench.
body:
• The Supreme Court on Wednesday stayed investigation in the CMRL-Exalogic FIR against former Kerala Chief Minister Pinarayi Vijayan, his daughter Veena T and her husband P A Mohamed Riyas for one week.
  • A vacation bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana set aside the Kerala High Court division bench's refusal of leave to appeal, so the three can challenge the single judge's October 9 FIR direction on merits.
  • The FIR stays in existence — only the investigation is paused. The court said its observations go only to the right to appeal, not to the merits.
  • The underlying allegation is that CMRL paid Rs 2.78 crore to Veena's now-defunct Exalogic Solutions as IT consultancy fees, which the ED flagged to state police.

The Supreme Court on Wednesday stayed for one week the investigation against former Kerala Chief Minister Pinarayi Vijayan, his daughter Veena T and her husband P A Mohamed Riyas in the alleged Cochin Minerals and Rutile Limited (CMRL) bribery case, allowing them to appeal to a division bench of the Kerala High Court.

A vacation bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana clarified that the first information report (FIR) will remain in existence but no investigation will proceed for a week, according to Bar and Bench and The Hindu BusinessLine. The bench set aside the High Court division bench's October 15 order refusing the three leave to appeal.

How the Case Reached the Supreme Court

On October 9, a single judge of the Kerala High Court directed the state's Vigilance and Anti-Corruption Bureau (VACB) to register a case based on a report the Enforcement Directorate (ED) had submitted to state police after its investigation and searches under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA). The VACB's Special Investigation Unit-1 then registered two FIRs against Vijayan and family members.

https://x.com/barandbench/status/2112809588584251673

Vijayan, Veena and Riyas said they were not heard by the single judge before that direction, and that the petition decided on October 9 was in the form of a public interest litigation that should have been heard by a division bench. On October 15, the division bench rejected their applications to appeal, holding, in the formulation reported by BusinessLine, that "an accused in a corruption case has no legal right to be heard before registering the FIR." They then moved the Supreme Court in Pinarayi Vijayan v Adv KM Shajahan and others.

The ED's allegation is that CMRL made payments of Rs 2.78 crore to Exalogic Solutions, Veena's now-defunct company, under the guise of IT consultancy services. The allegations have not been established in a trial.

What the Supreme Court Said

The bench took exception to the High Court acting in haste. It noted the state had already constituted a Special Investigation Team (SIT) to conduct a preliminary inquiry after receiving the ED's information, and questioned why a court should direct immediate FIR registration without letting that process run or hearing the persons affected.

"The FIR is registered. That is it. We will allow the FIR to exist, but we will stall the investigation. Don't use the process of statutory powers to meddle into the statutory domain of other entities."

— Supreme Court bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana

The court cautioned the ED against extending beyond its statutory limits under Section 66(2) of the PMLA, and questioned whether such information, read with Vijay Madanlal Choudhary, automatically obliges a state agency to register an FIR — an issue left for the division bench.

The Other Side: ED and the Complainant

The ED and the original complainant argued the opposite position, and the bench recorded it. Senior Advocate Zoheb Hossain, for the ED, submitted that the evidence disclosed cognizable offences. Counsel for complainant K M Shajahan — the lawyer-activist whose petition led to the October 9 order — argued that Vijay Madanlal Choudhary makes registration mandatory once the ED forwards a recommendation, and said he had approached the High Court after two representations asking the state to act on the Section 66(2) communication.

For Vijayan, Senior Advocates Sidharth Luthra and N Hariharan argued the single judge decided without hearing the 82-year-old former chief minister, and that Section 66(2) is not a blanket mandate. The court said it was "unable to agree" that the accused have no right to appeal, stressing its observations were limited to locus and "not an expression of opinion on merits."

What's Next

Vijayan, Veena and Riyas have one week to pursue their appeal before the division bench and seek interim relief there, including on whether a Section 66(2) communication compels FIR registration. Until then, the FIR exists and the allegations remain untested — Wednesday changed procedure, not the underlying case.
